lines.text: Why did a McDonald's hamburger cost fifteen cents in the nineteen-fifties, but costs several dollars today?
The burger didn't get ten times bigger or more delicious; the value of your dollar shrank.
This steady price increase is called inflation, and it happens when money supply outpaces real goods.
When central banks expand money and credit, more dollars compete for the same supply of eggs, oil, and homes.
Producers face rising wages and shipping costs, passing those expenses directly to grocery shelf price tags.
A healthy economy targets two percent annual inflation to encourage people to invest and spend rather than hoard cash.
To beat inflation, always invest your savings in assets that grow faster than the money supply.
